one_liner: C++17 HTTP/1.1 web framework on Seastar's thread-per-core reactor; 5-14% more plaintext req/s than actix-web 2.0 at 100 connections.
what_it_does: A small web framework layered on Seastar: you build a cpv::Application from modules (logging, HTTP server, routing) with a dependency-injection container, and register future-returning handlers on exact or wildcard (*, **) paths, or chain your own middleware-style handlers. It includes HTTP/1.0/1.1 with pipelining, streaming request and response bodies, a static-file handler (pre-compressed .gz, Range, If-Modified-Since, LRU cache), and JSON (sajson) and form serializers. It is a separate C++ framework, not an actix-web replacement: code is written as Seastar future chains and runs inside seastar::app_template.
how_it_is_fast: It inherits Seastar's shared-nothing, shard-per-core model: services are instantiated on every core with --smp and never shared, so the request path takes no locks and uses no atomics. Requests are parsed with a vendored Node.js http-parser 2.9.2, and the URL, headers, query values and body come out as cpv::SharedString, a reference-counted slice of the received seastar::temporary_buffer, so nothing is copied except in edge cases (headers split across packets, decoded query strings). Responses are built as cpv::Packet scatter lists of static and shared fragments and written with vectored I/O. Smaller tricks: a per-thread Date header cached per second, thread-local Reusable<T> free-list pools for per-request stream objects, and separate receive and reply loops per connection for pipelining, with a synchronous fast path when the flush future is already ready.
when_to_use: You already run Seastar shard-per-core services on Linux and want routing, DI, static files and JSON on the same reactor, not a separate HTTP stack.
Small plaintext or JSON responses over keep-alive or pipelined HTTP/1.1 on a few pinned cores, where per-core req/s matters (84.7k req/s on one 2011-era Xeon core in the author's test).
You are willing to vendor it and port it yourself: 148 commented .cpp/.hpp files (~690 KB including the vendored http-parser and sajson) on a pinned 2019 Seastar snapshot.
As a reference design for zero-copy HTTP/1.1 parsing with ref-counted buffer slices and scatter-gather responses.
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs TLS, HTTP/2, an HTTP client or a reverse proxy: the 0.3 roadmap items (http client, ssl) never shipped, a reverse-proxy request (#15) was deferred to that release, and #17 (proxy, http2) is unanswered.

Production services that need maintenance: no code commits since 2020-01-21, packages exist only for Ubuntu 18.04 with Seastar 20191017.1, and an open 2022 issue (#26) reporting a segfault inside libCPVFramework.so when running the hello-world example has no maintainer reply.
Chasing maximum Seastar throughput: on the author's own page plain seastar-httpd beat cpv-framework in all six throughput configurations (e.g. 184.5k vs 170.6k req/s at 2 cores/100 connections).
Comparing with a current actix-web: only actix-web 2.0.0 was measured, and cpv-framework already lost at 2 cores/10k connections (136.7k vs 141.5k req/s).
macOS or Windows hosts, or code that can't be restructured into non-blocking future chains (C++20 coroutine support is only a backlog item).

integration.dependencies: Seastar (via pkg-config 'seastar'; the author's PPA ships snapshot 20191017.1); vendored Node.js http-parser 2.9.2 and sajson; GoogleTest for tests only
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, GCC 9 (g++-9), CMake 3.8+; library built with -O3 -flto and the gold linker
integration.platforms: Linux only (the README says to use a Docker Ubuntu 18.04 image on Windows/macOS); Debian package is amd64 for Ubuntu 18.04 (bionic)
integration.thread_safety: Shared-nothing by design: each core runs its own copy of services, so handler code on a shard needs no locks, but nothing protects state you share across cores yourself; not otherwise documented

gotchas: Keep-alive is dropped if a response has neither Content-Length nor chunked Transfer-Encoding, if Content-Length doesn't match the bytes written (logged as a warning), or if the handler didn't fully consume the request body.

Default per-request limits: 512 KB and 512 packets for headers plus initial body (exceeding either returns 400 and closes), a 60 s timeout applied to every read and write, and a queue of 100 pipelined requests per connection; change them via HttpServerConfiguration.
Reusable<T> keeps thread-local free lists (32768/sizeof(T) slots per type), and its header warns that keeping a Reusable<> alive after freeResources can segfault.

The handler docs still show the pre-0.2 signature (const HttpServerRequestHandlerIterator&), but 0.2 changed it to pass by value. Every connection close is logged at Info, so raising the default Notice-level console logger to Info floods output under connection churn.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Drogon, Crow or Oat++ only when your process is already a Seastar shard-per-core application and you'd rather maintain an abandoned framework than write routing on top of seastar-httpd. For a maintained C++ HTTP server with TLS, HTTP/2 or clients, Drogon, H2O or Sogou Workflow are the safer choices.
verified_claims_summary: The author's wiki run of 2020-01-21 was a single 4-core Xeon E31225 @ 3.10GHz host, with the server pinned to 1-2 cores and wrk/wrk2 pinned to cores 2-3 over loopback, best of 3. cpv-framework 0.2.0.0 (g++-9 Release, epoll backend) served a 'Hello World!' GET at 84.7k vs 80.5k req/s against actix-web 2.0.0 (cargo --release, rustc unstated) on 1 core/100 connections (~1.05x) and 170.6k vs 149.6k on 2 cores (~1.14x), lost at 2 cores/10k connections, and its 1.2-2x wins at 20k connections coincide with actix returning 158k-178k non-2xx responses; the fixed-rate wrk2 latencies were indistinguishable across all servers.
status_note: Abandoned: the last code commit and 0.2 tag are from January 2020, and later pushes are only dependabot branches. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but it is tied to GCC 9 and a 2019 Seastar snapshot, so expect to port it to current Seastar yourself.
